skill_title: Describe magnetic fields, poles and the Earth's magnetic field

items.question: What happens when the north pole of one magnet is brought near the north pole of another?
items.expectedAnswer: They repel each other.
items.explanation: Like poles repel; two north poles push apart.
options: They repel each other.
They attract each other.
Nothing happens.

items.question: What happens when the north pole of one magnet is brought near the south pole of another?
items.expectedAnswer: They attract each other.
items.explanation: Unlike poles (north–south) attract.
options: They repel each other.
They attract each other.
Nothing happens.

items.question: Outside a bar magnet, in which direction do the magnetic field lines point?
items.expectedAnswer: From the north pole to the south pole.
items.explanation: By convention, field lines run from N to S outside the magnet.
options: From the south pole to the north pole.
Into both poles.
From the north pole to the south pole.

items.question: Can two magnetic field lines ever cross each other?
items.expectedAnswer: No — field lines never cross.
items.explanation: Magnetic field lines never cross; a crossing would mean two field directions at one point.
options: No — field lines never cross.
Yes — they cross at the poles.
Yes — they cross midway between magnets.

items.question: Where is a bar magnet's magnetic field strongest?
items.expectedAnswer: At the poles, where the field lines are closest together.
items.explanation: Closely spaced field lines at the poles indicate the strongest field.
options: In the middle of the magnet.
At the poles, where the field lines are closest together.
It is the same strength everywhere.

items.question: What does the closeness (density) of magnetic field lines show?
items.expectedAnswer: How strong the field is (closer lines = stronger field).
items.explanation: The spacing of field lines represents field strength: closer = stronger.
options: How fast the magnet is moving.
The temperature of the magnet.
How strong the field is (closer lines = stronger field).

items.question: Why does a freely suspended bar magnet always come to rest pointing roughly north–south?
items.expectedAnswer: It lines up with the Earth's magnetic field.
items.explanation: The Earth acts like a giant magnet, so a free magnet aligns with the Earth's field (a compass).
options: It lines up with the Earth's magnetic field.
It is pulled by the Sun.
It is repelled by all metals.

items.question: A compass needle is itself a small...
items.expectedAnswer: magnet.
items.explanation: A compass needle is a small magnet free to rotate and align with a magnetic field.
options: battery.
magnet.
electric charge.

items.question: Two unlike poles are placed near each other. How are the field lines between them arranged?
items.expectedAnswer: They run directly from the north pole across to the south pole.
items.explanation: Between unlike poles the field lines link N to S directly (an attractive pattern).
options: They point away from each other.
There are no field lines between them.
They run directly from the north pole across to the south pole.

items.question: Which material is magnetic (attracted to a magnet)?
items.expectedAnswer: Iron
items.explanation: Iron (and steel, nickel, cobalt) is magnetic; copper and wood are not.
options: Iron
Copper
Wood

items.question: Inside a bar magnet, the field lines point...
items.expectedAnswer: from the south pole to the north pole (completing a loop).
items.explanation: Field lines form closed loops: N→S outside, and S→N inside the magnet.
options: from the north pole to the south pole.
from the south pole to the north pole (completing a loop).
they stop at the poles.

items.question: A compass is placed near a bar magnet's north pole. Which way does the compass's north (red) end point?
items.expectedAnswer: Away from the magnet's north pole (it is repelled).
items.explanation: Like poles repel, so the compass north end points away from the magnet's north pole, along the field.
options: Towards the magnet's north pole.
It spins continuously.
Away from the magnet's north pole (it is repelled).

items.question: The Earth's magnetic field behaves as if there is a bar magnet inside the Earth. Where is this imaginary magnet's SOUTH pole?
items.expectedAnswer: Near the Earth's geographic NORTH.
items.explanation: A compass north points geographically north because the Earth's magnetic south is near the geographic north.
options: Near the Earth's geographic NORTH.
Near the Earth's geographic south.
At the centre of the Earth only.

items.question: Why does a compass needle's north end point towards the Earth's geographic north?
items.expectedAnswer: The Earth's magnetic south pole lies near the geographic north, attracting the needle's north end.
items.explanation: Unlike poles attract: the compass north is drawn to the Earth's magnetic south, located near geographic north.
options: The geographic north is also a magnetic north pole.
The Earth's magnetic south pole lies near the geographic north, attracting the needle's north end.
The needle is attracted to the cold.

items.question: Two bar magnets are placed end to end with field lines that seem to push apart and avoid each other between them. Which poles face each other?
items.expectedAnswer: Two like poles (e.g. N and N).
items.explanation: Like poles repel, producing a field pattern where lines push apart with a neutral point between.
options: A north and a south pole.
It is impossible to tell.
Two like poles (e.g. N and N).

items.question: What is a 'neutral point' in a magnetic field?
items.expectedAnswer: A point where the magnetic fields cancel and the net field is zero.
items.explanation: At a neutral point the fields from different sources cancel, giving zero net field.
options: A point where the magnetic fields cancel and the net field is zero.
The strongest point of the field.
The centre of a single magnet.

items.question: You have an unmarked bar magnet and a compass. How can you identify the magnet's north pole?
items.expectedAnswer: The compass end that points to the Earth's north is its north; the magnet pole that repels it is north.
items.explanation: The compass north end is repelled by the magnet's north pole (like poles repel), identifying it.
options: The pole that attracts the compass north end is north.
The compass end that points to the Earth's north is its north; the magnet pole that repels it is north.
Both poles attract the compass equally.

items.question: Iron filings sprinkled around a bar magnet line up to show...
items.expectedAnswer: the shape and direction of the magnetic field.
items.explanation: Iron filings become tiny magnets and align along the field lines, revealing the field pattern.
options: the electric current in the magnet.
the weight of the magnet.
the shape and direction of the magnetic field.

items.question: Which statement about magnetic poles is correct?
items.expectedAnswer: Poles always occur in north–south pairs; a single isolated pole has never been found.
items.explanation: Magnetic poles always come in pairs; cutting a magnet makes two smaller magnets, each with N and S.
options: Poles always occur in north–south pairs; a single isolated pole has never been found.
You can have a magnet with only a north pole.
Cutting a magnet in half removes one pole.

items.question: A magnet is cut in half across its middle. What are the two pieces?
items.expectedAnswer: Two complete magnets, each with its own north and south pole.
items.explanation: Each half becomes a full magnet with both poles — isolated single poles do not exist.
options: One north-only and one south-only magnet.
Two complete magnets, each with its own north and south pole.
Two non-magnetic pieces.
